```{r}
#| label: fly-setup
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

# Validation-fold results copied from the DEP_ML_FP repo (results/); nothing typed in by hand.
lb <- read_csv("../VizCode/FlyReservoir/leaderboard.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
mk <- read_csv("../VizCode/FlyReservoir/memory_by_kind.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ridge_skill <- lb |> filter(model == "ridge") |> pull(`skill vs naive`)

gap <- mk |>
  select(horizon, model, rmse = `all rows`) |>
  group_by(horizon) |>
  mutate(
    A = rmse[str_starts(model, "A:")],   # ridge on current-month values only
    B = rmse[str_starts(model, "B:")]    # ridge on all 28 history features
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!str_starts(model, "A:"), !str_starts(model, "B:")) |>
  mutate(closed = (A - rmse) / (A - B))

pct <- function(x, d = 0) percent(x, accuracy = 10^-d)
```

## Question

Does the wiring of the *Drosophila* mushroom body, used as a fixed recurrent network (a reservoir), forecast armed conflict better than random networks and conventional models?

## Design

Monthly state-based conflict deaths (UCDP GED, country-month panel, 1989-2025) are forecast at horizons of 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. The reservoir is a leaky echo-state network wired as the fly's mushroom body plus the olfactory projection neurons that feed it (FlyWire). In Tier 1 every connection is frozen and only a linear readout is trained, which is the cleanest test of whether the wiring itself helps. Control networks (weight-shuffled, degree-preserving rewired, random) get identical tuning budgets, validation uses five expanding-window rolling-origin folds, and 2021-2025 is held out as a locked test set.

## Findings

**Conventional baselines.** Ridge regression on 28 hand-built history features beats a tuned moving-average baseline by `r pct(min(ridge_skill), 1)` to `r pct(max(ridge_skill), 1)` in RMSE across horizons; random forest and gradient boosting never reliably beat ridge.

```{r}
#| label: fly-leaderboard
#| echo: false
lb |>
  select(Horizon = horizon, model, rmse) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rmse) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mean validation RMSE on log(1 + deaths), by horizon (months)")
```

**The reservoirs supply memory, but the fly's wiring adds nothing.** With history-free inputs, the reservoirs must create the memory themselves. Across horizons, the fly and its three control networks close `r pct(min(gap$closed))` to `r pct(max(gap$closed))` of the gap between ridge on current values and ridge on full history, and the fly is indistinguishable from the controls.

```{r}
#| label: fly-gap
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 7
gap |>
  mutate(is_fly = model == "fly") |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(horizon), closed, colour = model, shape = is_fly)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 17, `FALSE` = 16), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Forecast horizon (months)",
    y = "Share of the history gap closed",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Fly wiring vs. control networks",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: ridge regression with the full set of history features"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

**The mechanism is leaky averaging, not recurrence.** Linear reservoirs do at least as well as nonlinear ones, a bank of unconnected leaky units ties every network, and plain exponential moving averages of the inputs land within rounding of the reservoirs. The 96 mushroom-body output neurons read out worse than 96 random units.

> *A fixed fly-connectome reservoir recovers nearly all the forecasting skill that explicit history provides, but so does a random network, a bank of unconnected leaky units, and a set of exponential moving averages.*
